components.note: 女 (woman) — 姐 names a female relative, an older sister.
且 (qiě) gives the rhyme, close to jiě though the tone differs.
女 (woman) — 姐 names a female relative, an older sister.
且 (qiě) gives the rhyme, close to jiě though the tone differs.

example.hanzi: 我姐姐在北京工作。
example.pinyin: Wǒ jiějie zài Běijīng gōngzuò.
example.english: My older sister works in Beijing.
example.fact: Chinese kinship terms encode relative age in a way English doesn't bother to: 姐姐 can only mean an OLDER sister, and a younger one is a completely different word, 妹妹 — English "sister" covers both without distinction, so learners have to relearn the concept of "sister" as inherently ranked.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 浪 names movement on the surface of water, a wave.
良 (liáng) gives a rhyme close to làng, with a different initial and tone.
贝 (shell/money) — 费 relates to spending money, fees, and expenses
弗 (fú) gives a loose sound connection to 费's reading fèi

example.hanzi: 别浪费时间,快点做作业。
example.pinyin: Bié làngfèi shíjiān, kuài diǎn zuò zuòyè.
example.english: Don't waste time, hurry and do your homework.
example.fact: 浪费 can take almost any resource as its object — time, money, food, talent, an opportunity — functioning much like English "waste." Its more colloquial cousin 白费 ("to expend in vain," as in 白费力气) narrows in specifically on effort spent with nothing gained, a slightly different shade of the same basic idea.

components.note: 夕 (evening/night), doubled — two nights stacked together suggested the idea of accumulation, giving 多 its meaning of 'many, much.'
讠 (speech) — 谢 describes an act of speaking, giving thanks.
射 (shè) gives the sound — an exact match with 谢.

example.hanzi: 多谢你的帮助。
example.pinyin: Duōxiè nǐ de bāngzhù.
example.english: Many thanks for your help.
example.fact: 多谢 literally reads as "many thanks" — 多 ("many") intensifying 谢 ("to thank") the same way 非常 intensifies adjectives elsewhere in this deck. In standard Mandarin it can feel a touch more formal than 谢谢; in Cantonese, the same two characters (read do1 ze6) are simply the everyday, default way to say "thank you."

components.note: 女 depicts a kneeling figure with arms crossed, a traditional posture — a simple picture of a woman.
月, appearing twice side by side, originally depicted two people (or two strings of shells) together — giving 朋 its meaning 'friend, companion.'
又 (hand), shown twice and joined together — two hands clasped in friendship gave 友 its meaning 'friend.'

example.hanzi: 这是我的女朋友。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ de nǚpéngyou.
example.english: This is my girlfriend.
example.fact: 朋友 already means "friend" on its own; adding 女 ("female") narrows it specifically to a romantic girlfriend, the same modification pattern that gives 男朋友 (also in this batch) for "boyfriend." Because of that romantic narrowing, a plain female friend has to be called something else, like 女性朋友, to avoid the girlfriend implication.

components.note: 力 (strength/force) — 动 relates to movement produced by exertion or force.
牛 (ox/cattle) — cattle were among the earliest and most valuable kinds of property, connecting 物 to the general idea of 'object' or 'thing.'
勿 (wù) gives the sound — 物 is also pronounced wù, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 熊猫是一种很可爱的动物。
example.pinyin: Xióngmāo shì yì zhǒng hěn kě'ài de dòngwù.
example.english: The panda is a very cute kind of animal.
example.fact: 动物 is built from 动 ("to move") plus 物 ("thing, object") — quite transparent logic: "a moving thing." It forms a clean pair with 植物 ("plant," literally "a planted thing"), the basic two-way split Chinese uses to sort living things by whether they move on their own.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
牛 (ox/cow) — cattle were used to help split or divide things such as firewood.
丷 depicts two small pieces splitting apart — giving 半 its meaning 'half.'

example.hanzi: 这块蛋糕的一半是我的。
example.pinyin: Zhè kuài dàngāo de yíbàn shì wǒ de.
example.english: Half of this cake is mine.
example.fact: 一半 is one of the few fraction expressions used constantly in everyday speech rather than saved for math class — a full fraction in Chinese normally follows the pattern X分之Y (三分之一, "a third"), but "half" skips that whole template because 半 already means "half" outright.

components.note: 甘 (sweet) — describes the fruit's taste.
木 (tree) — the sweet fruit of an unspecified tree gave 某 its meaning 'a certain, some.'
丨 (a vertical tally mark) over 人 (person) — suggests counting people one by one, fitting 个's role today as Mandarin's most common general measure word.

example.hanzi: 我好像在某个地方见过他。
example.pinyin: Wǒ hǎoxiàng zài mǒu ge dìfang jiànguò tā.
example.english: I feel like I've seen him somewhere before.
example.fact: 某 deliberately keeps a person, place, or thing vague — 某个地方 ("somewhere"), 某个人 ("someone"), 某天 ("one day") — acting as Mandarin's built-in "unspecified X" slot, much like English "a certain" or "some" placed before a noun without committing to details.

example.hanzi: 他为何迟迟不回复?
example.pinyin: Tā wèihé chíchí bù huífù?
example.english: Why hasn't he replied for so long?
example.fact: 为何 is a more literary, formal cousin of the everyday 为什么 — 何 alone is a classical-Chinese question word for "what, which," so 为何 shows up far more in writing, news headlines, and formal speech, while 为什么 dominates ordinary conversation.

components.note: 女 (woman) with 覀 depicting hands on the waist — an old image of insisting or demanding something, connected to 要's meaning 'to want, to need.'

example.hanzi: 要么你来,要么我去。
example.pinyin: Yàome nǐ lái, yàome wǒ qù.
example.english: Either you come, or I go.
example.fact: 要么 almost always appears twice in a row as a paired construction — "要么...,要么..." ("either... or...") — laying out two alternatives, much like English "either...or." Using it only once, without a matching partner, reads as incomplete to a native speaker.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 试 relates to proposing or trying something out
式 (shì) gives the sound — an exact match with 试's pronunciation shì
图 is the simplified form of 圖, which pictured a district's borders 啚 enclosed within a boundary 囗 — an old image of a map, giving 图 its meaning 'picture, chart, map.'

example.hanzi: 警方试图找到失踪的男孩。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng shìtú zhǎodào shīzōng de nánhái.
example.english: The police attempted to find the missing boy.
example.fact: 试图 leans formal and shows up constantly in news reports about an ongoing or failed effort. In everyday speech, Mandarin speakers reach instead for the plainer 想 ("want to") or 试着 ("try to"), saving 试图 for a more deliberate, often unsuccessful attempt.

components.note: 厂 (a cliff or overhang) — 反 pictures pushing against a steep surface.
又 (a hand) — a hand pushing back against a cliff gave 反 its meaning 'to turn over' or 'opposite.'

example.hanzi: 他听到这个消息后,没有任何反应。
example.pinyin: Tā tīngdào zhège xiāoxi hòu, méiyǒu rènhé fǎnyìng.
example.english: He had no reaction at all after hearing this news.
example.fact: 反应 covers both a person's emotional or physical reaction and a chemical reaction (化学反应) with the exact same word — English sometimes reaches for different terms across those registers, but Mandarin's 反应 spans both without needing a separate word.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
辶 (walking/movement) — links 边's meaning to a boundary or edge one moves along.
臱 (biān) gives the sound — 边 is also pronounced biān, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 他一边吃饭,一边看手机。
example.pinyin: Tā yìbiān chīfàn, yìbiān kàn shǒujī.
example.english: He eats while looking at his phone.
example.fact: Doubled as "一边...,一边...", it marks two actions happening at the same time ("while...") — a purely grammatical role quite far from its literal meaning "one side," the same kind of drift that turned 一起 (also in this deck) from a literal "rising together" into the abstract "together."

components.note: 口 (mouth) — words spoken by a mouth are what reach the ear, giving 听 its meaning 'to listen.'
斤 stands in for the ear in this simplified character — the target that spoken words reach.
冂 (a simplified eye shape in 见's modern form) — emphasizes the act of seeing.
儿 (a person) — a person with an emphasized eye above gives 见 its meaning 'to see.'

example.hanzi: 我没听见你说的话。
example.pinyin: Wǒ méi tīngjiàn nǐ shuō de huà.
example.english: I didn't hear what you said.
example.fact: 听见 pairs the plain action verb 听 ("to listen") with the result complement 见 ("to succeed in perceiving") — grammatically parallel to 看见 ("to see," literally "look" plus "succeed in perceiving"). Chinese frequently needs an added complement like this to confirm an action actually succeeded, since 听 alone only means "to listen," not that the sound was actually caught.

components.note: 舍 (house) — 舒 relates to a sense of settled, at-ease comfort, 'relaxed, comfortable.'
予 (yǔ) is only distantly related in sound to shū — the connection has drifted apart over time.
卩 (a person) — the one being dressed.
月 (a garment shape) — a hand 又 placing a coat on the person, giving 服 its meaning 'clothes; to obey, submit.'

example.hanzi: 这张床睡起来很舒服。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhāng chuáng shuì qǐlai hěn shūfu.
example.english: This bed is very comfortable to sleep on.
example.fact: 不舒服 is also the everyday, mild way to say "I feel unwell, under the weather" — a common trap for learners who expect a dedicated word for illness but instead just find the negated form of "comfortable."

components.note: 丿 (something falling) — an object slipping away.
夫 (a hand/person) — the object slipping out of a hand, giving 失 its meaning 'to lose.'
攵 (a striking hand) — 败 relates to being struck down or defeated.
贝 (bèi) gives a sound close to bài, sharing the same initial.

example.hanzi: 这次考试他又失败了。
example.pinyin: Zhè cì kǎoshì tā yòu shībài le.
example.english: He failed this exam again.
example.fact: 失败 pairs two near-synonyms that each independently evoke loss or defeat — 失 ("to lose") and 败 ("to be defeated") — reinforcing each other into one stronger word, the same word-building strategy behind 喜欢 and 应该 from earlier in this deck.

components.note: 月 (yuè) here actually derives from 肉 (meat) — 有 originally depicted a hand holding meat, meaning 'to possess'; it also lends a loose phonetic connection to yǒu.
日 (sun/day) — relates to 时's meaning of 'time, season'; the phonetic part of the character was later replaced by 寸 in the simplified form

example.hanzi: 我有时会一个人去看电影。
example.pinyin: Wǒ yǒushí huì yí gè rén qù kàn diànyǐng.
example.english: Sometimes I go watch movies alone.
example.fact: 有时 is a shortened, slightly more literary version of the fuller 有时候 ("there are times when") — both mean "sometimes," but 有时 turns up more in writing, while spoken Mandarin leans toward 有时候 or its close cousin 有的时候.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
舟 (boat/tray) — represents a vessel or tray holding items.
殳 (a hand with a tool) — sorting or moving items on a tray gave 般 its meaning 'sort, kind, manner.'

example.hanzi: 他一般七点起床。
example.pinyin: Tā yìbān qī diǎn qǐchuáng.
example.english: He usually gets up at seven.
example.fact: 一般 as an adverb before a verb means "usually, generally" (一般来说, "generally speaking"), while as an adjective before a noun it means "ordinary, so-so" (一般的电影, "a so-so movie") — one word doing two related but distinct grammatical jobs, disambiguated only by its position in the sentence.

components.note: 人 (person) forms the top of the character.
八, shown here as a dividing line, suggests separation or a boundary — together with 人 above, giving 介 its meaning 'to lie between, to introduce.'
纟 (thread) — 绍 originally related to connecting threads, extended to mean 'to continue, carry on' and 'to introduce.'
召 (zhào) gives a sound close to shào.

example.hanzi: 让我介绍一下我的家人。
example.pinyin: Ràng wǒ jièshào yíxià wǒ de jiārén.
example.english: Let me introduce my family.
example.fact: 介绍 nearly always shows up with 一下 tacked on right after it (介绍一下, "let me introduce...") — 一下 softens the request into something casual and brief, the same verb-softening pattern that 一下's own entry in this deck describes.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.
夕 (evening, night) — divination was traditionally done in the evening.
卜 (to divine, reading cracks in bone or shell) — combined with 夕 (evening), an evening divination was for unusual or 'outside' matters, giving 外 its meaning of 'outside' or 'foreign.'

example.hanzi: 这次的结果让大家都很意外。
example.pinyin: Zhè cì de jiéguǒ ràng dàjiā dōu hěn yìwài.
example.english: This result surprised everyone.
example.fact: 意外 works as both an adjective ("unexpected, surprising") and a noun ("an accident, a mishap") without changing form — so 出意外 ("something went wrong") uses the noun sense, while 很意外 ("very surprising") uses the adjective sense of the exact same word.

components.note: 责 shows 贝 (money, a cowry shell) at its base, tied to a debt that must be repaid — giving 责 its meaning 'duty, responsibility, to blame.'
亻 (person) — 任 relates to a person taking on a responsibility or role.
壬 (rén) gives a hint of the sound — 任 is pronounced rèn, a connection that has shifted somewhat.

example.hanzi: 照顾孩子是父母的责任。
example.pinyin: Zhàogù háizi shì fùmǔ de zérèn.
example.english: Taking care of children is parents' responsibility.
example.fact: 负责任 ("to bear responsibility, to be responsible") is the verb phrase built on top of the noun 责任 — Chinese frequently turns an abstract noun into an action by adding a light verb like 负 ("to carry, bear") in front of it, rather than switching to a wholly different word the way English distinguishes "responsibility" from "to be responsible."

components.note: 人 — a lid covering the dish
良 — a dish piled with food
牛 (ox/cattle) — cattle were among the earliest and most valuable kinds of property, connecting 物 to the general idea of 'object' or 'thing.'
勿 (wù) gives the sound — 物 is also pronounced wù, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 冰箱里没有食物了。
example.pinyin: Bīngxiāng lǐ méiyǒu shíwù le.
example.english: There's no food left in the fridge.
example.fact: 食物 is the general, slightly formal word for "food" as a category. Casual speech instead reaches for 东西 (also in this deck) in the fixed phrase 吃东西 ("to eat [something]"), while a specific dish is called 菜 — three overlapping words for eating that aren't freely interchangeable.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 洛 names a river.
各 (gè) gives a sound close to luò, sharing a related rhyme.
木 (tree) — 杉 names a type of coniferous tree, the fir or cedar.
彡 (shān) gives the sound — an exact match with 杉.
石 (stone) — the stone radical, marking the character as related to rock or stone.
几 (jǐ) gives a sound close to 矶's reading jī — the same syllable, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 我朋友住在洛杉矶。
example.pinyin: Wǒ péngyou zhù zài Luòshānjī.
example.english: My friend lives in Los Angeles.
example.fact: 洛杉矶 is a phonetic transliteration of "Los Angeles," its three characters chosen mainly for sound rather than meaning — 矶 (jī, "a rocky shoal by the water") is a fairly obscure character otherwise, kept alive in everyday use largely because of this one high-frequency city name.

components.note: 辶 (to walk, to move) — suggests departing or leaving.
贵 (valuable, precious) — leaving something valuable behind gave 遗 its meaning 'to lose, to leave behind.'
忄 (heart) — 憾 describes an emotional sense of regret or dissatisfaction.
感 (gǎn) gives a sound close to hàn, sharing the rhyme -an.

example.hanzi: 没能参加你的婚礼,我很遗憾。
example.pinyin: Méi néng cānjiā nǐ de hūnlǐ, wǒ hěn yíhàn.
example.english: I regret not being able to attend your wedding.
example.fact: 遗憾 describes regret over something outside one's control — a missed opportunity, bad luck, someone else's loss — while 后悔 is reserved for regretting one's own choice or action. English "regret" blurs the two together, but mixing them up is a common tell of a learner.

meanings: to come over from the enemy's side

components.note: 厂 (a cliff or overhang) — 反 pictures pushing against a steep surface.
又 (a hand) — a hand pushing back against a cliff gave 反 its meaning 'to turn over' or 'opposite.'
一 (a line, representing a target or standard) — 正 shows a foot arriving exactly at the right mark.
止 (foot, to stop) — arriving and stopping precisely at the target gives 正 its meaning of 'correct' or 'straight.'

example.hanzi: 算了吧,反正你说了他也不会听。
example.pinyin: Suànle ba, fǎnzhèng nǐ shuō le tā yě bú huì tīng.
example.english: Forget it — he won't listen anyway even if you say something.
example.fact: Beyond its everyday sense of "anyway, regardless," dictionaries also carry an older, specialized meaning for 反正 — "to defect, to come over to the correct/legitimate side" — a more literal reading of its two characters (反 "to turn against" + 正 "correct, legitimate") that survives from a more formal historical and political register.

components.note: 乂 depicts crossed strokes suggesting a cutting action.
木 (wood) here represents a wooden stake — giving 杀 its meaning 'to kill.'
手 is a simple picture of an open hand with the fingers spread out.

example.hanzi: 电影里的杀手最后被警察抓住了。
example.pinyin: Diànyǐng lǐ de shāshǒu zuìhòu bèi jǐngchá zhuāzhù le.
example.english: The killer in the movie was finally caught by the police.
example.fact: 杀手 also extends into a common, casual metaphor for anything that "kills" something non-literally — 时间杀手 ("a time-killer," something that eats up huge amounts of time) is a frequent coinage built the same way English calls an addictive game or show "a real time-killer."

components.note: 讠 (speech) — relates to 设's meaning 'to establish, set up,' something first proposed through words.
殳 (shū) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from shè.
讠 (speech) — 计 relates to counting or planning through words and numbers.
十 (shí) gives a hint of the sound — 计 is pronounced jì, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 这个网站是我朋友设计的。
example.pinyin: Zhège wǎngzhàn shì wǒ péngyou shèjì de.
example.english: This website was designed by my friend.
example.fact: 设计 functions as both verb and noun without changing form, joining a long list of Chinese words with this flexibility already seen in this deck (工作, 意外) — English marks the difference between "to design" and "a design," while Chinese relies entirely on sentence position.

components.note: Money/shell — winning is linked to gaining wealth or profit.
寸 (a hand) reaching for 旦 (originally 貝, a shell used as currency) — a picture of grasping something valuable, hence 'to obtain, to get.'

example.hanzi: 这个球队赢得了冠军。
example.pinyin: Zhège qiúduì yíngdé le guànjūn.
example.english: This team won the championship.
example.fact: 赢得 is a more formal, written-register pairing than the plain verb 赢 alone — 赢 by itself already means "to win" and can stand alone in speech (赢了! "Won!"), while 赢得 almost always needs a following object (赢得冠军, 赢得尊重) and reads noticeably more like news writing than casual talk.

components.note: 一 (a line, representing a target or standard) — 正 shows a foot arriving exactly at the right mark.
止 (foot, to stop) — arriving and stopping precisely at the target gives 正 its meaning of 'correct' or 'straight.'
Traditionally analyzed as 日 combined with 疋, linked to the idea of speaking directly and truthfully — the source of 是's meaning 'to be, indeed, right.'

example.hanzi: 这正是我想要的答案。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhèngshì wǒ xiǎng yào de dá'àn.
example.english: This is exactly the answer I wanted.
example.fact: 正是 intensifies the plain copula 是 ("to be") with 正 ("precisely, exactly right") in front of it — functioning much like 就是 (also in this deck) as an emphatic "is exactly." 正 and 就 work as near-interchangeable intensifiers Mandarin uses constantly to sharpen an otherwise plain statement of identity.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — the act of speaking.
正 (straight, correct) — speaking the straight, correct truth, giving 证 its meaning 'to prove, certify; evidence.'
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 警察正在寻找目击证人。
example.pinyin: Jǐngchá zhèngzài xúnzhǎo mùjī zhèngrén.
example.english: The police are looking for eyewitnesses.
example.fact: 证人 is built from 证 ("to prove, evidence") plus 人 ("person") — literally "a proof-person." It's the same logical pattern behind many Chinese role nouns that fuse a function directly onto 人, like 主人 ("host/owner," literally "master-person") or 客人 ("guest," literally "guest-person").

components.note: 羊 (sheep; here representing feathers or ornaments on a headdress) — an elaborate decoration worn on the head.
大 (a person, arms outstretched) — a person wearing a decorated headdress was seen as beautiful, giving 美 its meaning 'beautiful.'
丽 is the simplified form of 麗, which depicted the ornate antlers of a deer (鹿) — a fitting image behind its meaning 'beautiful, magnificent.'

example.hanzi: 这是一座美丽的城市。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì yí zuò měilì de chéngshì.
example.english: This is a beautiful city.
example.fact: 美丽 leans literary and is mainly reserved for describing scenery, cities, or a formal kind of beauty — for everyday, all-purpose "pretty, good-looking," spoken Mandarin overwhelmingly prefers the shorter, more casual 好看 or 漂亮 instead.

components.note: 土 (soil) — earth being pressed down
厂 (a cliff/overhang) — a heavy mass bearing down from above
力 depicts the blade of a plow — since plowing fields took great physical effort, the shape came to represent strength or power.

example.hanzi: 工作压力太大,他每天都很累。
example.pinyin: Gōngzuò yālì tài dà, tā měitiān dōu hěn lèi.
example.english: Work pressure is too much; he's tired every day.
example.fact: 压力 covers both literal physical pressure (as in physics or engineering) and figurative psychological stress with the same word — 有压力 ("to be under pressure, stressed") is one of the most common ways Chinese speakers today describe work or study-related stress.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 味 relates to taste, sensed in the mouth.
未 (wèi) gives the sound — an exact match with 味.
辶 (to walk) — 道 relates to a path or road one walks along.
首 (shǒu) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer resembles dào, a reminder that sound components can drift after thousands of years of pronunciation change.

example.hanzi: 这个汤的味道很好。
example.pinyin: Zhège tāng de wèidao hěn hǎo.
example.english: This soup tastes great.
example.fact: 味道 extends past literal taste into a figurative "sense, feel, vibe" of a situation — 有点味道 can describe an interesting or nuanced quality in music, writing, or a place, much like English stretches "flavor" beyond food ("a certain flavor to the writing").

components.note: 氵 (water) — 淘 originally described washing something in water.
匋 (táo) gives the sound — an exact match with 淘.
氵 (water) — 汰 originally described washing or rinsing away.
太 (tài) gives the sound — an exact match with 汰's reading.

example.hanzi: 他在第一轮比赛就被淘汰了。
example.pinyin: Tā zài dì yī lún bǐsài jiù bèi táotài le.
example.english: He was eliminated in the very first round of the competition.
example.fact: 淘汰 combines two water-related verbs — 淘 ("to wash, to rinse," as in panning for gold) and 汰 ("to rinse away, to wash out") — into a vivid image of impurities being washed out, which is exactly how it's used today for eliminating a weaker competitor, product, or outdated technology.

example.hanzi: 你的中文说得真厉害!
example.pinyin: Nǐ de Zhōngwén shuō de zhēn lìhai!
example.english: Your Chinese is really amazing!
example.fact: 厉害 swings between two very different registers depending on context — as praise it means "amazing, impressive" (你真厉害, "you're awesome"), but attached to pain, weather, or an illness it means "severe, intense" (疼得很厉害, "hurts a lot") — the same word covering both a compliment and a complaint.

meanings: sb with whom one has a close personal relationship

components.note: 禾 (grain) — grain was one of the first things ancient people owned and kept for themselves.
厶 pictures something folded in on itself and hidden away, giving 私 its sense of 'private, personal, one's own.'
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 这是我的私人物品,请不要动。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ de sīrén wùpǐn, qǐng búyào dòng.
example.english: These are my private belongings, please don't touch them.
example.fact: 私人 pairs with a following noun to mark it as personal or private property — 私人医生 ("private doctor"), 私人时间 ("personal time"). The single character 私 already carries the "private, personal" sense on its own, as in 私立 ("privately run," e.g. of schools), but 私人 is the form used to modify another noun.

components.note: 屮 (a young sprout) growing up and out of 凵 (a container or pit) — a picture of something emerging, hence 'going out.'

example.hanzi: 我们明天早上八点出发。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen míngtiān zǎoshang bā diǎn chūfā.
example.english: We're setting off at eight tomorrow morning.
example.fact: 出发 combines 出 ("to go out") with 发 ("to send off, to issue") into the literal image of "sending oneself out" on a journey — the same 发 shows up in 发车 ("a vehicle departs") and 出发点 ("starting point," also used figuratively for a starting premise in an argument).

components.note: 亻 (person) — 伟 describes a person of great, extraordinary character.
韦 (wéi) gives a sound close to wěi, sharing the same syllable body and differing mainly in tone.
A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'

example.hanzi: 他是一位伟大的科学家。
example.pinyin: Tā shì yí wèi wěidà de kēxuéjiā.
example.english: He is a great scientist.
example.fact: 伟大 is reserved for genuinely momentous, history-scale greatness — a great leader, a great achievement, a great civilization — and sounds oddly over-the-top applied to something merely very good, a register mismatch that trips up learners; that everyday-compliment job instead falls to 很棒 or 太好了.

components.note: 大 (a person) — arms spread, exerting effort.
田 (a field) — working hard on the land, together giving 奋 its meaning 'to strive, exert oneself.'

example.hanzi: 听到这个好消息,她非常兴奋。
example.pinyin: Tīngdào zhège hǎo xiāoxi, tā fēicháng xīngfèn.
example.english: Hearing this good news, she was extremely excited.
example.fact: 兴奋 describes a heightened, almost physiological state of excitement — strong enough that 兴奋剂 (literally "excitement agent") is the standard Chinese term for a stimulant or performance-enhancing drug, a more clinical use of the same root than the everyday "excited" sense suggests.

components.note: 见 (to see) — the act of looking.
又 (again, or a hand) — looking closely or repeatedly, giving 观 its meaning 'to observe, view.'
人 (person), tripled — three people together depict a crowd, giving 众 its meaning 'many, multitude.'

example.hanzi: 电影结束后,观众都站起来鼓掌。
example.pinyin: Diànyǐng jiéshù hòu, guānzhòng dōu zhàn qǐlai gǔzhǎng.
example.english: After the movie ended, the audience all stood up and applauded.
example.fact: 观众 literally combines 观 ("to watch, observe") with 众 ("crowd, multitude") into "watching crowd." The same 众 appears in 群众 ("the masses") and 大众 ("the public"), a recurring building block for words describing groups of people.

components.note: A picture of a nose; because people in ancient China would point to their own nose when referring to themselves, the character came to mean 'self.'
人 (person), doubled — one person shown following another depicts the idea of accompanying or coming from somewhere.

example.hanzi: 自从上大学以后,我很少回家。
example.pinyin: Zìcóng shàng dàxué yǐhòu, wǒ hěn shǎo huí jiā.
example.english: Since starting university, I've rarely gone home.
example.fact: 自从 almost always sets up a time-clause that gets closed out later by 以后 or 就 ("自从...以后, ..." / "自从...,就..."), marking a change that began at a point in the past and continues into the present — dropping the second half can leave the sentence feeling grammatically unfinished to a native ear.

components.note: A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.
弓 (bow) — 弹 relates to a projectile shot from a bow, like a pellet
单 (dān) gives a loose sound connection to 弹's reading dàn

example.hanzi: 他的枪里已经没有子弹了。
example.pinyin: Tā de qiāng lǐ yǐjīng méiyǒu zǐdàn le.
example.english: There are no more bullets left in his gun.
example.fact: 弹 is a heteronym: read dàn it means a small round projectile (子弹 "bullet," 炸弹 "bomb"), but read tán it means "to pluck, to play (a string instrument)" as in 弹钢琴 ("to play the piano") — the same character, two completely different pronunciations and meanings depending on what's attached to it.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 垃 relates to piled-up waste or debris on the ground.
立 (lì) gives a sound distantly related to lā, having drifted apart over time.
土 (earth) — 圾 relates to loose earth or debris; it survives only as half of a compound word.
及 (jí) gives a sound close to jī, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 请把垃圾扔进垃圾桶。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ lājī rēng jìn lājītǒng.
example.english: Please throw the trash into the trash can.
example.fact: Mainland Mandarin says lājī, but Taiwan Mandarin traditionally pronounces the very same two characters lèsè — a rare case where two major regional standards diverge sharply enough in pronunciation that the word can sound almost unrelated despite being written identically.

components.note: 小 (small, young) — 叔 describes a younger member of the family.
又 (a hand) — historically part of a scene of picking beans; today it simply combines with 小 to give 叔 its meaning 'a younger uncle.'
小 (small, young) — 叔 describes a younger member of the family.
又 (a hand) — historically part of a scene of picking beans; today it simply combines with 小 to give 叔 its meaning 'a younger uncle.'

example.hanzi: 那个叔叔在公园里遛狗。
example.pinyin: Nàge shūshu zài gōngyuán lǐ liù gǒu.
example.english: That man is walking his dog in the park.
example.fact: Beyond its precise kinship meaning ("father's younger brother"), 叔叔 also doubles as a polite, generic way for a child to address or refer to an unrelated adult man roughly a parent's age — parallel to how 阿姨 ("auntie") works for women — a common way Chinese kinship terms extend outward into everyday social titles.

components.note: 田 (field) — represents farmland.
力 (strength/effort) — someone strong enough to work the fields gave 男 its meaning 'male, man.'
月, appearing twice side by side, originally depicted two people (or two strings of shells) together — giving 朋 its meaning 'friend, companion.'
又 (hand), shown twice and joined together — two hands clasped in friendship gave 友 its meaning 'friend.'

example.hanzi: 她带男朋友回家见父母。
example.pinyin: Tā dài nánpéngyou huí jiā jiàn fùmǔ.
example.english: She brought her boyfriend home to meet her parents.
example.fact: 男朋友 mirrors 女朋友 (also in this deck) exactly, swapping only the gender character 男 for 女 in front of the shared root 朋友 ("friend") — a simple, symmetric pattern Mandarin reuses across many gendered pairs, like 男生/女生 ("male/female student") and 男老师/女老师 ("male/female teacher").

components.note: 龶 depicts a poisonous plant, tying 毒 to its meaning 'poison.'
母 (mǔ) gives a rhyme close to dú, with the initial shifted.
口 (mouth), stacked three times — many mouths talking about or judging something, the source of 品's meaning 'product, item; quality, rank.'

example.hanzi: 贩卖毒品是严重的犯罪行为。
example.pinyin: Fànmài dúpǐn shì yánzhòng de fànzuì xíngwéi.
example.english: Selling drugs is a serious crime.
example.fact: 毒品 narrows the broader character 毒 ("poison, toxic") down specifically to illegal narcotics by adding 品 ("product, item"). The same 品 turns other roots into product categories, like 食品 ("food product") or 商品 ("merchandise") — a recurring word-formation slot for "a category of goods."

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'

example.hanzi: 你不必担心我,我可以照顾自己。
example.pinyin: Nǐ búbì dānxīn wǒ, wǒ kěyǐ zhàogù zìjǐ.
example.english: You don't need to worry about me, I can take care of myself.
example.fact: 不必 is a more formal, compact alternative to 不需要 ("don't need to") — both mean "there's no need to," but 不必 fits into a single beat before the verb, so it turns up constantly in polite reassurances like 不必客气 ("no need to be so polite," a formal cousin of 不用谢).

components.note: 厂 (a cliff or overhang) — 反 pictures pushing against a steep surface.
又 (a hand) — a hand pushing back against a cliff gave 反 its meaning 'to turn over' or 'opposite.'
又 (hand) and 寸 (also derived from a hand shape) — together suggesting two hands matching or corresponding, related to 对's meaning 'correct, matching.'

example.hanzi: 很多人反对这个新规定。
example.pinyin: Hěn duō rén fǎnduì zhège xīn guīdìng.
example.english: Many people oppose this new regulation.
example.fact: 反对 is built from 反 ("opposite, to turn against") plus 对 ("correct, to face") — literally "to turn against what's correct." Its direct antonym 赞成 ("to approve, to support") is the word most often taught right alongside it, forming one of Mandarin's cleanest opposite pairs.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 停 relates to a person coming to a halt
亭 (tíng) gives the sound — an exact match with 停's reading tíng
A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.

example.hanzi: 车突然停下了。
example.pinyin: Chē tūrán tíng xià le.
example.english: The car suddenly stopped.
example.fact: 停下 attaches the directional complement 下 ("down") to the plain verb 停 ("to stop") to emphasize a full, physical halt in motion — it contrasts with the more formal, abstract 停止, which is used for stopping an activity or process rather than a moving object.

meanings: to test (a person's skill in a particular area)

components.note: 氵 (water) — 测 originally referred to measuring the depth of water.
则 (zé) gives a rhyme close to cè, with the tone and initial shifted.
讠 (speech) — 试 relates to proposing or trying something out
式 (shì) gives the sound — an exact match with 试's pronunciation shì

example.hanzi: 这个软件还在测试阶段。
example.pinyin: Zhège ruǎnjiàn hái zài cèshì jiēduàn.
example.english: This software is still in the testing phase.
example.fact: 测试 leans technical and is the standard word for testing software, machinery, or a hypothesis, while testing a person's classroom knowledge more often reaches for 测验 or the everyday 考试 ("exam") — three overlapping "test" words roughly sorted by what's actually being tested.

components.note: 米 (grain, especially husked rice) — 精's meaning 'refined, essence, spirit' relates to rice refined to its purest form.
青 (qīng) gives a sound hint — 精 is pronounced jīng, sharing the same rhyme though the initial consonant differs.
彡 (fine lines, streaks) — 彩 relates to patterns and bright colors.
采 (cǎi) gives the sound — an exact match with 彩's reading cǎi.

example.hanzi: 这场比赛真精彩!
example.pinyin: Zhè chǎng bǐsài zhēn jīngcǎi!
example.english: This match was truly brilliant!
example.fact: 精彩 praises the quality of a performance, show, speech, or match — vivid, skillful, and engaging — rather than a person's character. A movie, a goal, or a talk can be 精彩, but calling a person 精彩 sounds like an odd, non-standard compliment; 精彩 sticks to describing performances and moments.
